bibliography.checked_against: the title page (PDF p. 3) and copyright page (PDF p. 4)
bibliography.note: Title page: 'Stages in the Development of Ictalurus nebulosus', by Philip B. Armstrong, M.D., College of Medicine at Syracuse, State University of New York, and Marine Biological Laboratory, Woods Hole; illustrated by Julia Swope Child; Syracuse University Press 1962 (LC card 63-11037). The entry agrees. The text proper is printed pp. [3]–8 plus plates.

claims.paper: Table 3.6-1 (brown bullhead, eggs; row sources include Armstrong 1962)
claims.quote: from several hundred up to a thousand and more eggs in a single egg mass
claims.conditions: general description of egg masses collected in nature (central New York and Cape Cod); no counts given

claims.quote: The eggs measure about 3 mm. in diameter.
claims.conditions: 'Those from the same egg mass are remarkably uniform in size but there are differences in size from one egg mass to another'; the subchorionic space is about one-third of the egg's diameter

claims.claim: eggs laid in an excavation or burrow
claims.quote: an open shallow excavation among weeds, or a burrow excavated by the adults
claims.conditions: '… under the roots of a water plant'; burrows run 'horizontally for as much as three feet into the bank'; also pails, stovepipes, tires, cinder blocks, under boards or stones; nest floor firm (coarse sand, gravel or stone)
claims.note: The excavation-or-burrow part is in Armstrong. The 0.2–1.2 m depth is not: Armstrong only advises setting drainage tiles 'in two or three feet of water' (0.6–0.9 m) for collectors. The depth range comes from Breder 1939 (see that entry).

claims.claim: brown bullhead eggs die within about a day in still water (Breder 1935; Armstrong 1962)
claims.quote: eggs removed to still water usually will die within a day or so
claims.conditions: 'Apparently almost constant agitation is required to assure normal development of the eggs, since eggs removed to still water usually will die within a day or so'; a laboratory husbandry observation, no counts or temperatures; the adults fan the eggs and take them into their mouths (citing Breder 1935)
claims.note: Supports the project inference that the eggs depend on the parents' fanning; Armstrong also notes dead eggs 'quickly develop mold which extends to the adjacent eggs and kills them'.

notes: Armstrong gives no spawning temperature, depth range, care split or hatch length (the row's 'after a slow rise to ~21 °C', '0.2–1.2 m', 'both parents in 56 %' and 'hatch 7–8 mm' come from its other sources). Other values: the laying season starts about the middle of May in central New York and on Cape Cod; the latest newly laid eggs on Cape Cod were found on 28 July (p. 4, PDF p. 6); after yolk absorption the young swim 'as a compact school in shallow water guarded by the adults' for a few days, then disperse to deeper water (p. 5, PDF p. 7); development to Stage 53 (yolk absorbed, adult pattern) takes 17 days at 20–21 °C (p. 7, PDF p. 9). INCUBATION: the row's '6–10 d (mean 8) at 21.3 °C' is Breder 1939's (not checked here as Armstrong's), but Armstrong independently gives hatching (Stage 43) at 8 days at 20–21 °C in running tap water in the laboratory, most embryos of a mass emerging within three to four hours ('At 20 to 21° C. the development described above through Stage 53 is completed in seventeen days', with the time table: Stage 43, 8 days; p. 7, PDF p. 9). That agrees with the mean of 8 d and can be cited beside Breder.
